sections.section_title: Initial Clinical Approach: Acute Neck Swelling with Subtle Myopathy Clues
sections.description: Framework for evaluating acute cervical swelling when deep neck infection and classic angioedema are excluded, emphasizing recognition of dermatomyositis (DM)–related pseudoangioedema and early clues to inflammatory myopathy.
key_points: Differentiate true angioedema (histaminergic vs bradykinin-mediated) from inflammatory or structural mimics based on timing, triggers, urticaria, pain, pruritus, family history, medication exposures (ACE inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors), and response to epinephrine/antihistamines.

Identify red flags for myositis masquerading as angioedema: subacute course, painless nonpitting edema, proximal muscle weakness, dysphagia, hoarseness/cough with secretions, and characteristic rashes or periungual changes.
Perform targeted skin and nailfold examination for heliotrope, Gottron’s papules, shawl/V-neck/Holster signs, periungual erythema, and nailfold capillary abnormalities.

Order early muscle injury labs in atypical angioedema presentations: creatine kinase (CK), aldolase, AST/ALT (disproportionately elevated from muscle), and LDH; assess renal function and urine myoglobin.
Use imaging and airway assessment to exclude ENT emergencies: contrast-enhanced CT neck for deep space infection; flexible nasoendoscopy for airway patency and secretion management.
Avoid anchoring bias—normal C1 esterase inhibitor level/function and normal C4 argue against bradykinin-mediated angioedema and should prompt consideration of inflammatory myopathy.
Recognize extrathoracic restrictive physiology on pulmonary function testing (PFTs) as a clue to oropharyngeal/laryngeal muscle involvement.
Engage multidisciplinary input early (ED, ENT, immunology/rheumatology, neurology, speech-language pathology) for airway safety and expedited diagnosis.

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology and Serologic Phenotypes of Dermatomyositis (SAE1-Positive Focus)
sections.description: Mechanisms of tissue injury in DM and the clinical phenotype associated with anti–small ubiquitin-like modifier activating enzyme (SAE1) antibodies.
key_points: DM is a complement-mediated microangiopathy: immune complexes activate complement with membrane attack complex (C5b-9) deposition in endomysial capillaries, driving ischemic perifascicular myofiber injury.
Type I interferon signaling is a hallmark, contributing to endothelial injury, muscle damage, and characteristic skin manifestations.
Cutaneous features include heliotrope rash, Gottron’s papules/sign, shawl/V-neck and Holster signs, periungual telangiectasias/erythema; edema may be prominent but is uncommon.

Extramuscular involvement: dysphagia from pharyngeal/upper esophageal muscle weakness; interstitial lung disease (ILD); aspiration pneumonitis; cardiac involvement (arrhythmias, myocarditis) less common but important.
SAE1-positive DM phenotype: frequent prominent cutaneous disease, substantial rates of dysphagia (~40–50%) and ILD (~40%), and a measurable malignancy association (~15–20%).
Subcutaneous edema (“pseudoangioedema”) reflects inflammatory capillary leak and myofasciitis; although reported more often with MDA5 and TIF1-γ antibodies, it can occur with SAE1.
Serum muscle enzymes vary from mild to marked elevations; CK can be very high during active myositis.
Muscle biopsy typically shows perifascicular atrophy/necrosis, perimysial/perivascular inflammation, and C5b-9 deposition—findings that support DM over other inflammatory myopathies.

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis: Cervical Swelling, Dysphagia, and Weakness
sections.description: Systematic differential for neck edema with oropharyngeal symptoms and weakness, highlighting discriminating clinical and laboratory features.
key_points: Angioedema: histaminergic (often pruritic, urticaria, rapid onset, antihistamine-responsive) vs bradykinin-mediated (ACE inhibitor–related, hereditary/acquired C1-INH deficiency with low C4 and abnormal C1-INH).
Infections/inflammation: Ludwig angina, deep neck space infection/abscess, bacterial sialadenitis, cellulitis/erysipelas; usually febrile with leukocytosis, focal pain, and imaging evidence.
Neuromuscular junction: myasthenia gravis (fatigable bulbar weakness, normal CK), botulism (autonomic signs); EMG and serologies assist.

Other inflammatory myopathies: immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (anti-HMGCR/anti-SRP; marked CK; minimal rash), inclusion body myositis (older age, distal finger flexor/quadriceps weakness, dysphagia; biopsy rimmed vacuoles), overlap/antisynthetase syndrome (mechanic’s hands, ILD, arthritis).
Endocrine/metabolic/toxic: hypothyroid myopathy, drug/toxin-induced rhabdomyolysis (e.g., statins), electrolyte disorders.
Allergic/toxic dermatoses: DRESS, acute contact dermatitis (painful, pruritic, often exudative).
Vascular/structural: superior vena cava syndrome (facial plethora, venous distention), goiter, neoplasm, lymphatic obstruction, orofacial granulomatosis, sarcoidosis.
Discriminators: CK and muscle enzyme pattern, autoantibodies, complement/C1-INH panel, imaging (CT/MRI), EMG, biopsy, presence of pathognomonic DM rashes and nailfold capillary changes.

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup of Suspected Dermatomyositis with Neck Edema
sections.description: Stepwise testing to confirm DM, assess severity and distribution, exclude mimics, and screen for associated conditions (ILD and malignancy).
key_points: Core laboratories: CK, aldolase, AST/ALT, LDH; inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR); urinalysis for myoglobin; renal function to monitor rhabdomyolysis risk.

Autoimmunity testing: ANA (often positive, speckled); comprehensive myositis-specific antibody panel (e.g., SAE1, Mi-2, TIF1-γ, MDA5, NXP2, Jo-1 and other antisynthetases, SRP, HMGCR) to define phenotype and prognosis.
Angioedema panel when indicated: C4, C1-INH antigen/function; serum tryptase if anaphylaxis suspected—normal studies support pseudoangioedema rather than bradykinin-mediated disease.
Muscle imaging: MRI of symptomatic muscle groups to detect edema and guide biopsy; FDG-PET can quantify inflammatory burden and concurrently survey for occult malignancy.
Pulmonary assessment: high-resolution CT chest for ILD; PFTs with spirometry and DLCO; recognize extrathoracic restriction suggesting upper airway involvement.
Swallowing assessment: videofluoroscopic swallow study to quantify pharyngeal dysfunction and aspiration risk; guides nutrition and airway management.
Histopathology: muscle biopsy showing perifascicular atrophy/necrosis, perimysial/perivascular inflammation, and C5b-9 capillary deposition confirms DM and excludes necrotizing myopathy/IBM.

Infection and immunization screen before immunosuppression: hepatitis B/C, HIV, TB testing; varicella-zoster serostatus; update non-live vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, recombinant zoster) when feasible.

Cancer risk stratification and screening: apply IMACS guidance—use clinical risk factors (e.g., DM phenotype, dysphagia, specific antibodies, age, sex) to select baseline imaging (CT or PET/CT), age-appropriate screenings, and targeted endoscopy; recognize limited sensitivity of tumor markers alone.
Baseline and serial monitoring: standardized muscle strength testing, CK trends, skin activity scores, pulmonary and swallowing reassessments to track response to therapy.

sections.section_title: Management of Dermatomyositis with Severe Oropharyngeal Involvement
sections.description: Evidence-informed therapeutic strategies for active DM manifesting with cervical edema and dysphagia, including immunomodulation, airway/nutrition support, and complication prevention.
key_points: Hospitalize patients with significant dysphagia, aspiration, or concern for airway compromise; coordinate with ENT and consider ICU monitoring if needed.
Glucocorticoids: pulse IV methylprednisolone for severe disease (e.g., 500–1000 mg daily for 3 days) followed by high-dose oral prednisone with gradual taper guided by clinical response and CK.
Steroid-sparing agents: select based on comorbidities and phenotype—mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate (caution with ILD), azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors; cyclophosphamide for severe ILD.
IVIG: effective for refractory muscle disease and dysphagia; consider loading dose (e.g., 2 g/kg) with maintenance cycles.
B-cell–directed therapy (e.g., rituximab) for refractory cases or when rapid steroid-sparing is needed.
Airway and dysphagia management: NGT or PEG for nutrition/hydration; aspiration precautions; intensive speech-language therapy with swallow rehabilitation.
Pulmonary care: treat aspiration pneumonitis; monitor for ILD progression; coordinate with pulmonology for immunosuppressive choices if ILD present.

Infection prophylaxis and safety: Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis during high-dose steroids or multi-agent therapy (TMP-SMX first-line; alternatives include atovaquone, dapsone with G6PD testing, or inhaled pentamidine); vaccinate with inactivated vaccines when possible before rituximab/IVIG; screen and manage latent infections.

Supportive care: bone protection (calcium/vitamin D, bisphosphonate as indicated), gastric ulcer prophylaxis when appropriate, venous thromboembolism prevention, glucose and blood pressure monitoring.
Rehabilitation: early PT/OT to restore strength and function while avoiding steroid myopathy; sun protection to limit cutaneous flares.
Response assessment and tapering: track CK, strength, swallowing function, and imaging; taper steroids slowly to minimize relapse; adjust steroid-sparing agents based on efficacy and tolerability.

sections.section_title: Prognosis, Malignancy Surveillance, and Clinical Pearls
sections.description: Expected clinical course, risks, and long-term monitoring with practical takeaways to avoid missed diagnoses and optimize outcomes.
key_points: Prognosis improves with early recognition and aggressive control of inflammation; severe dysphagia and extensive edema denote high disease activity but can remit with appropriate therapy.
SAE1-positive DM carries notable risks of dysphagia and ILD and a measurable association with malignancy; maintain vigilance even after initial negative screening.

Malignancy surveillance: baseline imaging (CT or PET/CT) and age-appropriate screenings at diagnosis; consider targeted endoscopy (e.g., upper/lower GI) based on risk and symptoms; reassess at intervals (e.g., within the first 3 years when risk is highest) or symptom-triggered thereafter.
Monitor for complications: aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, steroid toxicities, opportunistic infections, thromboembolism, cardiac involvement.

Medication monitoring: periodic CBC, LFTs, renal function for immunosuppressants; immunoglobulin levels and infection vigilance with rituximab; counsel on fertility/pregnancy considerations where relevant.
Patient education: recognize early signs of flare (new weakness, dysphagia, rash), adhere to therapy, photoprotection, vaccination planning, and prompt reporting of infections.

Clinical pearls: in “idiopathic angioedema” with normal C1-INH/C4, absent urticaria, and subacute course, check CK and carefully examine skin/nailfolds; pseudoangioedema can be the first clue to dermatomyositis.
Tumor markers alone are insufficient for cancer screening in DM; a structured, multimodal approach aligned with IMACS guidance is preferred.
